items.prompt: State what is meant by a computer network.
items.canonical_answer: A computer network is two or more computing devices connected together so that they can communicate and share data and resources.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - connected devices that communicate and share data and resources.

items.prompt: Explain why a school connects its computers into a network rather than leaving each machine stand-alone.
items.canonical_answer: Networked computers can share one printer and one file store instead of each needing its own, files move between users directly instead of travelling on a storage device by hand, and backups and security are managed centrally on the server rather than machine by machine. A stand-alone machine keeps its own copies and its own printer, so the school would buy the same hardware many times and manage each machine separately.
marking_guidance: Reason: one printer and one file store serve every machine - 1 mark.
Purpose: so files move directly and backup runs once centrally, because the network carries the data to one place instead of each user copying by hand - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: The receptionist's computer at a lodge must send a booking list to the manager's computer in another building on the same site. Explain what the lodge's network makes possible here.
items.canonical_answer: The lodge's network links the buildings' computers, so the receptionist sends the booking list directly over the network instead of carrying it on a storage device. The same infrastructure lets both computers share the lodge's printer and the booking file store, so each reaches the same data through the network it is joined to.
marking_guidance: Context: this lodge's two buildings on one site - 1 mark.
Reason: because the network carries the list between the machines, the sharing happens without hand-carried storage, so the receptionist and manager work from one joined system - 1 mark.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a local area network.
items.canonical_answer: A local area network (LAN) covers one small site, such as one building or campus, and is owned and managed by the organisation that uses it.

items.prompt: Explain why a bank's branches in Windhoek, Walvis Bay and Oshakati cannot all be joined as one LAN.
items.canonical_answer: The branches sit on separate sites many kilometres apart, and a LAN covers one small site such as a single building or campus, owned and run by one organisation. Sites that far apart are joined by a WAN, which spans a wide geographical area using long-distance links leased from communication providers, so distance is what rules out the single LAN.
marking_guidance: Reason: the branches are far apart on separate sites - 1 mark.
Purpose: so each site runs its own LAN and a WAN joins them, because the wide-area links a provider leases are what reach between towns - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A college has a campus in Keetmanshoop and a study centre 300 km away near Luederitz, and the two are linked. Explain why the linked network counts as a WAN.
items.canonical_answer: Each site’s devices form their own LAN, because each sits on one small site owned and run by the college. The link between the sites spans a wide geographical area and uses a provider’s long-distance line, which is what a WAN is, so the whole linked network of the college is a WAN made of two LANs.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the client-server model of networked computers.
items.canonical_answer: In the client-server model, server computers provide services, files and resources, and client computers request and use them over the network, with the server controlling access.

items.prompt: Explain why a school uses the client-server model for its learners' file storage.
items.canonical_answer: The server holds every learner's files in one place, so access is controlled centrally with one account per learner, backup runs once on the server instead of on every machine, and security is managed at one point. A peer-to-peer arrangement would leave each machine's files on that machine, so the school would have to trust and manage each one separately.

Purpose: so each learner reaches their own files through one account, because the server decides who may, which is what the model buys - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Four friends network their home computers to share films and one printer. Explain why the peer-to-peer model suits their network better than client-server.

For four machines with files to share, buying and running a server would cost more than the sharing is worth, which is why the peer-to-peer model fits this small home network.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a thin client.
items.canonical_answer: A thin client is a computer that depends on a server for its processing and storage: it sends requests and displays results while the server does the work.

items.prompt: Describe the difference between a thin client and a thick client.
items.canonical_answer: A thin client leaves processing and storage to a server, sending requests and displaying results, whereas a thick client does its own processing and storage locally, running its own applications and keeping its own files. A thin client depends on the server to work, while a thick client keeps working without one, so the two differ in where the work happens as well as what each needs.
marking_guidance: Difference: a thin client works through the server whereas a thick client works on its own - 1 mark per side, and both sides are needed, including that the work happens in different places.

items.prompt: A clinic's reception has an old computer that cannot run the new records software. Explain how a thin-client arrangement could let the reception still use it.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a network's topology.

items.prompt: Explain why a star topology is often chosen for a school computer room.
items.canonical_answer: Each computer connects by its own cable to one central switch, so one broken cable or one faulty machine strands exactly that one while the rest keep working, and the room gains simple management, since adding or removing a machine means plugging or unplugging one cable at the central device. The cost is one central device plus one cable per computer, and the risk is the central device itself, whose failure stops the whole room, which is the bargain the star offers.
marking_guidance: Reason: one cable per computer to one central device, so one fault strands one machine - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the room is simple to manage and cheap to cable, because every connection ends at the central switch, which is why schools choose the star - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Draw a star topology for a small office with four computers and one printer, showing every connection.
items.canonical_answer: One central device box, the switch. Four computer boxes and one printer box around it. One line from each computer to the switch and one line from the printer to the switch: five cables in all, and no line joins any computer to another directly, because in a star every connection passes through the central device.
marking_guidance: Context: this office with the given four computers and one printer - 1 mark for the central device with all five links ending at it, 1 mark for no direct device-to-device line.
Reason: each of the five cables ends at the switch, because a star connects every device to the central device and nothing else, so the pattern, not just the parts, earns the marks.

items.prompt: A learner draws a topology in which every computer connects to several of the others, and calls it a star. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: A star connects every device to one central device by its own cable, whereas a mesh connects each device to several of the others, so the drawing is of a mesh, whatever it is called. items.canonical_answer: A private cloud suits the clinic chain: the infrastructure is provided for that one organisation and is not shared with other customers, so the chain controls where patient records live and who administers the service. items.prompt: Describe the difference between wired and wireless network connections.
items.canonical_answer: A wired connection carries data through a physical cable, copper conducting electrical signals or fibre conducting light, so it is generally faster and more stable but needs cable laid to each device, whereas a wireless connection carries data by radio, so devices move freely with no cables laid, but performance varies with distance, walls and interference. Security differs with the medium too: a cable has to be physically tapped, while radio can be received by anyone within range.
marking_guidance: Difference: cable-conducted against radio-carried - 1 mark per side, whereas each side’s cost follows its medium, and both sides are needed.

items.prompt: A lodge's wi-fi reaches the rooms poorly through thick walls. Explain why a wired connection to each room's television would be more reliable.
items.canonical_answer: A cable carries its signal inside copper or fibre, so thick walls do not weaken it and nearby equipment does not disturb it, whereas radio weakens with distance and is absorbed and reflected by walls. Each television wired to the switch receives a stable signal, which is why the wired link is the more reliable of the two in this building.

items.canonical_answer: A NIC connects the device to the wired network, and what it carries that is fixed in the hardware is its own unique MAC address. The IP address is assigned by the network the device joins - by the network’s server or router - and can change when the device moves to another network, so it is not built into the card. The test: which address is fixed in the hardware? The MAC address; the IP address belongs to the network.

items.prompt: Explain why a school LAN that must reach the internet needs a router, not only a switch.
items.canonical_answer: A switch moves packets between devices on the one network it serves, but the school’s LAN and the internet are different networks, and joining networks is the router’s job: it forwards each packet toward the destination address on the other network. Without the router, the LAN’s packets would have no way off the school’s own network, which is why the router, not the switch, is the joining device.

items.prompt: A learner sends a photo from a hostel phone to a friend on another network in another town. Explain what the routers between them do.
items.canonical_answer: Each packet of the photo is read for its destination IP address, and each router along the way forwards it to the next network in the direction of that address, until a router on the friend’s own network delivers it. Packets of one photo may travel different routes, because each router chooses its own next step, so the friend’s device is what reassembles the packets into the picture.

items.prompt: Describe how CSMA/CD lets two devices share one Ethernet cable.
items.canonical_answer: Each device first listens to the cable and transmits only when it senses the cable is free, which is the carrier-sense step. While transmitting, it keeps listening; if two devices transmit together, the signals collide, both detect the collision, both stop, and each waits a different random time before sensing the cable and trying again, so the two retries do not collide.
marking_guidance: Order: the steps in sequence - sense first, then transmit, then detect and retry - each statement a mark point, up to 2 from a longer list.
Input: the process starts from a shared cable with devices ready to transmit.
Result: both devices get their data through, because the different random waits spread the retries.

items.prompt: Explain how a collision on an Ethernet cable is detected and dealt with.
items.canonical_answer: A transmitting device compares the signal on the cable with what it sent: a collision garbles the signal, so the difference is the detection. On detecting one, the device stops sending, sends a jamming signal so every other transmitter also stops, then waits a random time before sensing the cable and trying again, and the different random waits make the retries fall out of step, which is how the next attempt gets through.
marking_guidance: How the collision is found: the signal on the cable no longer matches what was sent - 1 mark.
Because each device stops, jams and waits a different random time, the retries separate, so the cable is shared without a manager - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A viewer starts a film on a rural connection whose bit rate is slower than the film's stream. Explain what the viewer sees.
items.canonical_answer: The bits arrive more slowly than the player consumes them, so the player’s store of bits runs out, playback stops, and the buffering mark appears until enough new bits have arrived to continue, which repeats until the end of the film. The connection’s bit rate, not the film’s size, is what sets this, so a lower-rate stream that fits the connection would play straight through.
marking_guidance: Context: this viewer's connection, slower than the given film stream - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Explain why IPv6 was introduced.
items.canonical_answer: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, giving about 4.3 thousand million combinations, and the world’s connected devices outnumbered them, so the pool of IPv4 addresses ran dry. IPv6 uses 128 bits, a vastly larger range written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, so every device can have its own address, which is the need that drove the introduction.
marking_guidance: Reason: the 32-bit IPv4 pool ran out against the number of connected devices - 1 mark.
Purpose: so IPv6 with its 128-bit range gives addresses in abundance, because the devices of the world needed more than 4.3 thousand million - 1 mark.

marking_guidance: Context: this school network’s addresses in the given table - 1 mark per completed entry, (a) IPv4, (b) IPv6, (c) public with the reason, (d) subnetting.

items.prompt: A learner says every device in the office LAN needs its own different public IP address. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Inside the office LAN the devices use private IP addresses, which work within the local network and are not unique on the internet; the router holds the office’s public IP address, which is unique on the internet, and speaks for the LAN outside. Public and private are different kinds of address: a device on the other side of the world can reach a public address directly, but no private one. The test: can a device far away reach it directly? Then it is public.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - private LAN addresses have been treated as needing to be public, a confusion of the two kinds.
1 mark: the correction with the test - private addresses serve inside the LAN, the router’s public address serves outside, and direct reachability from anywhere is the mark of a public address.

items.prompt: A learner writes an IPv6 address as six groups of hexadecimal digits separated by semicolons. Explain the errors.
items.canonical_answer: IPv6 addresses are eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, and a run of zero groups may be replaced by a double colon. Six groups is one slip and semicolons another: the separator is a colon, and the count is eight. The test: count the groups and check the separator - eight, colons - which the written address fails on both counts.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the group count and the separator are both wrong for IPv6, a confusion with another form of address.
1 mark: the correction with the test - eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, separated by colons, with a double colon for a run of zero groups.

items.prompt: Describe the three parts of the URL http://www.omatele.co.na/fees.htm.
items.canonical_answer: The scheme, http, names how the resource is fetched. The domain name, www.omatele.co.na, names the server that holds it. The file path, /fees.htm, names the file on that server. Reading the URL in order answers three questions in order: how to ask, whom to ask, and for what.

items.prompt: Explain how a browser uses the URL http://www.omatele.co.na/fees.htm to fetch a page.
items.canonical_answer: The browser reads the domain name, www.omatele.co.na, and finds that server’s IP address; then it sends a request for the file /fees.htm to that address using the scheme http; the server returns the page named by the path, and the browser displays it. Each part of the URL does one job in the fetch: the domain finds the machine, the path names the file, the scheme names the way of asking.
marking_guidance: How the fetch works: the domain is read first and its IP address found - 1 mark.
Because the request for the path’s file is sent in the scheme’s way, the page returns and is displayed, which is what each part contributes - 1 mark.

items.prompt:
The Tsandi Bush Lodge is fitting out its office: five computers on one site, one printer, a server holding the bookings, and guests who bring phones. The lodge is far from any fibre line and reaches the internet through the cell phone network.
(a) Identify two pieces of LAN hardware the lodge needs to connect its five computers and the printer, and one piece that lets the guests’ phones join. [2]
(b) The computers, printer and server all sit on the lodge’s own site. State what kind of network this is, and what kind of network the link to the internet belongs to. [2]
(c) The bookings are held on the lodge’s own server, and the reception computers request them. Explain the client-server benefit here. [2]
(d) Guests complain that the wi-fi drops out in the far rooms. Suggest, with a reason, one piece of hardware that would improve the far rooms’ signal. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A switch to connect the wired computers and the printer, network interface cards in each computer (or cables), and a wireless access point to let the guests’ phones join by radio - any two pieces for the computers plus the access point.
(b) The five computers, printer and server on one small site form a LAN, owned and run by the lodge; the link to the internet spans a wide area on a provider’s network, so it is part of a WAN - the internet is the largest example of one.
(c) The server holds every booking in one place, so access is controlled centrally, one backup covers all bookings, and a failure of one reception computer loses no data, because the records live on the server.
(d) A repeater: it takes the weakening signal and re-transmits it stronger, so the network reaches the far rooms without new cables.
marking_guidance: Part (a): identify the switch (and NICs or cables) plus the wireless access point - 2 points, one per identification.
Part (b): state the LAN for the site and the WAN for the internet link, because the size and ownership of each decides - 2 points.
Part (c): the reason the server helps this system - central control, one backup, no data lost with a client - 2 points.
Part (d): the context of the given far rooms - suggest the repeater with the reason that it re-transmits the signal stronger - 2 points.

items.prompt:
A guest’s booking request travels from a phone to the lodge’s booking server. The table shows the stages. Read the table and answer the questions.

| 1 | Guest’s phone | Sends the request by radio |
| 2 | Wireless access point | (a) |
| 3 | (b) | Sends each packet to the port of the device it is addressed to |
| 4 | Router | (c) |
| 5 | Booking server | Receives the request and replies |

(d) Explain, with a reason, why the request needs the router to leave the lodge’s network, and why the switch alone could not do that. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Lets the phone join the network by radio and passes its packets onto the wired LAN. (b) A switch. (c) Forwards the packets between the lodge’s network and the provider’s network, choosing the route by the destination IP address.
(d) The switch serves devices on the one LAN, moving packets between devices already on that network, but the booking request must leave the lodge’s network and travel to another, and joining networks is the router’s job: it forwards packets between networks by their destination IP addresses, so the request needs the router to get out.
marking_guidance: Read the given table: (a) the access point’s job with the phone joining by radio - 1 mark, (b) the switch - 1 mark, and (c) the router’s value as the answer that joins the networks - 1 mark.

Reason: (d) the switch serves one network whereas the router joins networks, because it forwards packets between networks by destination IP address - 3 marks, one per point: the switch’s limit, the router’s job, the mechanism that makes the difference.
